chapters.title: Three billion letters, two meters per nucleated cell
chapters.kicker: A book written in four letters, coiled inside nearly every cell.
chapters.cta: Open the viewer: 9 places in the genome

blocks.kid: Imagine a recipe book written with only four letters: A, C, G and T. The recipe book of your body is called DNA. It has about three billion letters. Imagine reading one letter every second, never sleeping, never stopping. One single copy would take you almost one hundred years. And your body holds two versions: one from your mum and one from your dad.
blocks.phd: T2T-CHM13 assembles 3.055 × 10⁹ bp of haploid sequence, with gapless assemblies for all chromosomes except Y, and the previous reference had left 8% of the genome unfinished (Nurk 2022). Build 35 (2004), which followed the first draft (Lander 2001), reached 2.85 × 10⁹ nucleotides with 341 gaps and about 99% of the euchromatin (IHGSC 2004). A G1 diploid nucleus therefore holds roughly 6.11 × 10⁹ bp (2 × 3.055 × 10⁹). This is our own calculation; it ignores XX/XY differences, the content of Y and individual structural variation.

blocks.kid: All of that book is coiled up inside almost every cell. Cells are the tiny living bricks of your body. They are too small to see. Stretch out the DNA thread of one cell and it would be about two meters long. That is nearly as tall as a door. A grown-up has around thirty million million cells. Nobody counted them one by one. It is a careful guess.
blocks.phd: DNA length per diploid nucleus is computed, not measured: 6.11 × 10⁹ bp × 0.335 nm/bp ≈ 2.04 m, our own calculation assuming a 2n nucleus. We measured the axial rise (3.35 Å per base pair) on the coordinates of the structure on screen, 1BNA: base-pair centers, principal-component axis, terminal pairs excluded. Drew 1981 supports the B-helix geometry (9.8 bp per turn). Sender 2016 estimate 3.0 × 10¹³ human cells in the 70 kg reference man; Bianconi 2013 estimate 3.72 × 10¹³ and note that earlier values spanned 10¹² to 10¹⁶. Multiplying gives 6.1–7.6 × 10¹³ m, a very loose upper bound rather than an estimate: many cells, such as mature erythrocytes, have no nucleus (the hematopoietic lineage is about 90% of cells; Sender 2016). Every nucleus is also assumed 2n, ignoring gametes (n) and S/G2 cells (up to 4n).

blocks.kid: Out of every hundred letters, only about {coding_pct} tell your body how to build its parts. Many of the other letters seem to work like light switches. They say when and where to use each recipe. Nobody knows yet how many switches there are. The whole book is called the genome.
blocks.phd: The protein-coding fraction is {coding_pct}% of the genome (declared range {coding_lo}–{coding_hi}% depending on isoform handling; computed here from GENCODE 50 CDS on the GRCh38 assembly, not taken from the literature; Frankish 2023 documents GENCODE, not this figure). Yet 88% of trait-associated SNPs in the 2009 GWAS catalog were intronic (45%) or intergenic (43%), although that share is not above expectation in introns and is depleted in intergenic regions (Hindorff 2009); associations concentrate instead in regulatory DNA marked by DNase I hypersensitive sites (Maurano 2012). How much of this non-coding DNA is functional remains contested and depends on the definition of function: ENCODE 2012 assigned biochemical function to ~80% of the genome, whereas Graur 2013 argues that the fraction under purifying selection is below 10%, and Christmas 2023 find ~10.7% (332 Mb) evolutionarily constrained across mammals; Kellis 2014 argue that biochemical, evolutionary and genetic approaches are complementary.

blocks.kid: Change one letter in a switch and a light might stay on when it should be off. A computer has learned to guess what such a change does. The Genome Viewer shows you those guesses. They are only guesses, not proofs: someone must check them in a laboratory.
blocks.phd: A deep-learning model from Google DeepMind (Avsec 2026) takes 1 Mb of sequence and predicts thousands of functional tracks at up to single-base-pair resolution, although current models often fail to predict the direction of effect of individual variants (Sasse 2023; Huang 2023). Sun 2026, a preprint without peer review, finds weak agreement between Borzoi and the DeepMind model and nominal eQTL effect sizes (Spearman ≤ 0.138), with better discrimination for variants at PIP ≥ 0.9; the authors recommend using such scores to prioritise, not as standalone predictors. The Genome Viewer shows those predictions, not measurements, for 9 loci.

chapters.title: The little that is translated, and all the rest
chapters.kicker: Most of your DNA holds no recipes for proteins, and it still seems to matter.
chapters.cta: Explore these regions in the Genome Viewer

blocks.kid: Think of your DNA as a giant cookbook. Only a few pages hold recipes. The recipes are for proteins, which are tiny parts of your body. A tiny machine called the ribosome reads a copy of each recipe and makes the part. Out of every 100 letters in the book, only about {coding_pct} are part of a recipe. Count it in other ways and you get between {coding_lo} and {coding_hi} out of 100. We counted this ourselves, letter by letter, using an official list of recipes.
blocks.phd: Protein-coding sequence is a small fraction of the genome. From GENCODE 50 (the project is described in Frankish 2023; the figure itself is ours and release-dependent) we merged the CDS of all isoforms into non-overlapping intervals (a base covered by ten transcripts counts once) and divided by the length of the GRCh38 primary assembly (chromosomes 1–22, X, Y and mitochondrial): {coding_pct}% of bases. The range {coding_lo}–{coding_hi}% spans the isoform sets (MANE Select, basic, all) and the two denominators (GRCh38 primary, T2T-CHM13). Adding the UTRs of the coding transcripts' exons, which are transcribed but not translated, raises the figure to {exons_pct}%: that is not the coding fraction and is not part of the range. The figure is computed rather than cited because it depends on the annotation release and on what is counted. The 2001 draft (Lander 2001) was the first draft sequence of the human genome; the 2004 report (IHGSC 2004) concluded that the genome seems to encode only 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes, an estimate of that date. The T2T-CHM13 assembly, gapless for all chromosomes except Y, is 3.055 billion base pairs (Nurk 2022).

blocks.kid: Some people called the rest of the book “junk DNA”, like an attic nobody climbs into. In 2012 a huge project called ENCODE said that 80 out of every 100 letters did something, like a fridge making a humming noise. Other scientists answered: making noise is not the same as cooling the food. By their count at the time, fewer than 10 out of every 100 letters stay almost the same across species, and that is a good clue they matter.
blocks.phd: Part of the sequence outside protein-coding genes was often summarised as “junk DNA”. ENCODE (2012) assigned biochemical function to 80% of the genome, particularly outside protein-coding regions; that is a claim about biochemical function, not selected-effect function. Graur et al. (2013) countered that ENCODE adopted the causal-role definition of function and inflated its estimates of functionality, putting the fraction conserved under purifying selection at less than 10%. Doolittle (2013), by a different route (the C-value paradox), argued that ENCODE's definition picks out many sites that standard biological usage would not call functional.

blocks.kid: Here is another clue: compare letters across 240 mammals, animals that feed their babies milk. If a letter hardly changes in almost any of them, it probably has a job. That is how scientists found that at least 10.7 out of every 100 human letters have barely changed. Of the ones that look well kept one by one, 8 out of 10 are not in recipes. Some may be like light switches that turn a recipe on or off. The Genome Viewer lets you explore this kind of letter.
blocks.phd: Zoonomia (Christmas 2023), aligning 240 mammal genomes, finds at least 332 Mb (~10.7%) of the human genome under evolutionary constraint, and 101 million significantly constrained single bases, 80% of them outside protein-coding exons. That is somewhat above the “less than 10%” bound Graur et al. (2013) gave for the fraction under purifying selection; the studies differ in year and method, so the figures are not directly comparable. This does not contradict the ~80% biochemical figure (ENCODE 2012): “function” has at least two readings. Selected-effect function: the element persists because of its fitness effect, with evolutionary constraint as the evidence. Causal role: it contributes to a system capacity, the definition Graur et al. (2013) say ENCODE used, typically evidenced by a reproducible biochemical assay signal. Whether active but nonconserved regions are functional remains open (Kellis 2014; Doolittle 2013).

chapters.title: How DNA is packed
chapters.kicker: DNA is not loose: it is wound up, and the more open the winding, the more readily it can be read.
chapters.cta: Open the track browser at a locus with a predicted accessibility signal

blocks.kid: Picture a thread so long it will not fit in your backpack. To store it, you wind it around tiny spools, like the ones in a sewing kit. Your DNA is like that thread: it holds the recipes for your body, and it gets wound up too. The spools sit one after another, strung on a cord. Then the cord is folded and pressed tight. That is how it fits inside every cell, a piece of your body too small to see.
blocks.phd: The basic packaging unit is the nucleosome: a histone octamer around which 146 base pairs (bp) of DNA are organized in a superhelix (Luger 1997, X-ray crystallography). The real structure shown in the Genome Viewer is a PDB entry; the exact DNA length is the one recorded in that entry. Consecutive nucleosomes, joined by linker DNA, form a chromatin fiber; how it folds into higher orders in vivo remains debated. As a rule, DNA wound on the octamer is less accessible to transcription factors than linker DNA (although pioneer factors can bind nucleosomal DNA); that difference is what the assays in the next block measure.

blocks.kid: But if the whole thread is wound up, how can it be read? It is much easier to read where the thread is loose, with no spool on top. Think of a library. Books on open shelves can be read. Books in closed boxes cannot. Scientists have a tool that cuts the thread only where it is loose. Then they count where the cuts landed. Where many cuts pile up, there are open shelves: places in the DNA that might be in use.
blocks.phd: Chromatin accessibility is inferred from which DNA is exposed to an enzyme. DNase-seq maps DNase I hypersensitive sites, which mark candidate regulatory elements; in primary human CD4+ T cells, Boyle 2008 reported 94,925 sites, of which only 16–21% lie in promoters or first exons; the rest lie elsewhere, many of them candidates for distal regulation. ATAC-seq uses a transposase and, in its original formulation, worked with 500–50,000 cells; besides open sites, it reveals DNA-binding proteins and nucleosome positions (Buenrostro 2013). Non-coding variants identified by GWAS concentrate in DNase I hypersensitive regions (Maurano 2012). Caveat: in bulk assays the signal is an average over a population of cells, and accessibility does not by itself demonstrate function.

blocks.kid: In the Genome Viewer, a map of DNA, there are some lines. Each line is a little mountain: the taller it is, the looser the thread is at that spot. We show two lines: one with the original DNA letter and one with a changed letter. If the mountain goes up or down, maybe that change opened or closed a shelf. Careful: nobody measured that mountain in a lab. It is drawn by an artificial-intelligence program from Google DeepMind that calculates what it would look like.
blocks.phd: The Genome Viewer's track browser (V3) shows predicted accessibility (ATAC and DNase) for the reference and alternative alleles at a locus. The predictions come from the model described in Avsec 2026 (Google DeepMind), which takes 1 Mb of sequence as input and predicts thousands of functional tracks at up to single-base-pair resolution; accessibility (ATAC, DNase) is one of its outputs. These are model predictions, not measurements. For gene expression, independent evaluations of earlier models show limited performance in explaining variation across individuals and frequent errors in the direction of effect (Huang 2023; Sasse 2023), and a recent non-peer-reviewed preprint (Sun 2026) finds weak agreement between AlphaGenome/Borzoi and eQTL effect sizes; none of these studies assesses accessibility. In any case, an ALT−REF accessibility difference is a hypothesis to be tested, not an observed effect.

chapters.title: The switches
chapters.kicker: Where a gene is switched on, and what switches it on from far away
chapters.cta: Open the tissue × modality map (body parts and signals) in the viewer

blocks.kid: Picture DNA as a giant recipe book. Before many recipes sits a "start" button, like on a blender. A small piece called TBP grabs that button. It bends the DNA, like a wire. The bend tells the machine that copies recipes: "start here." Look at the picture. It is a real structure: in a lab, people found where each tiny bit sits. That button is a switch. But in one kind of cell, only about 1 in 5 control spots sat next to a start button.
blocks.phd: The core promoter is the stretch of DNA around the transcription start site where the basal machinery positions RNA polymerase II. At TATA-containing promoters, TATA-binding protein (TBP) distorts the DNA on binding; PDB entry 1CDW, a human TBP–DNA complex, records that distortion in atomic coordinates (no bend angle is given here). PDB entry 5FLM, a mammalian elongation complex, shows the polymerase transcribing the template strand into RNA. In human CD4+ T cells, only 16–21% of 94,925 DNase I hypersensitive sites lay in promoters or first exons (Boyle 2008); the remainder includes candidate enhancers, silencers, insulators and locus control regions. That figure comes from a single cell type and should not be extrapolated genome-wide.

blocks.kid: Sometimes a switch sits far, far away from the lamp it turns on. Think of a button in the hallway. It lights a lamp on another floor through a cable hidden in the wall. DNA works the same way. One switch that helps build fingers sits a million letters away from the recipe it turns on. When a single letter in that switch changes, some people are born with extra fingers. Scientists saw this in four families that are not related.
blocks.phd: The ZRS lies within intron 5 of Lmbr1, 1 Mb from its target gene Shh; its point mutations cause preaxial polydactyly in four unrelated families (Lettice 2003). That distance is of the order of the model's 1 Mb input window (Avsec 2026). With the window centered on the element, each side reaches only half of it and Shh falls outside; only an off-center window, with the ZRS and Shh at its ends, would include both. Contacts are organized in topological domains (megabase-sized in Dixon 2012; median about 185 kb in Rao 2014). In the lymphoblastoid line GM12878, in situ Hi-C described about 10,000 loops that frequently link promoters and enhancers, and CTCF sites at loop anchors were convergent in more than 90% of cases (Rao 2014). At the EPHA4 locus, deletions, inversions and duplications that disrupt a CTCF-associated boundary rewire long-range enhancers and cause human limb malformations (Lupiáñez 2015). These references do not by themselves demonstrate the ZRS–Shh loop.

blocks.kid: Another switch sits in a region called FTO. One changed letter makes two recipes glow twice as bright. This happens in lab-grown fat cells that are still maturing. They used to burn energy; now they store it and give off five times less heat. The viewer has a map. Each row is a part of the body. Each column is a kind of signal: a trace that DNA leaves when it works. The map shows what a computer program works out in advance, not what anyone measured.
blocks.phd: At the FTO locus, the variant rs1421085 (T>C) disrupts a conserved ARID5B repressor motif and doubles IRX3 and IRX5 expression during early adipocyte differentiation; it shifts beige adipocytes toward white and reduces mitochondrial thermogenesis five-fold. IRX3/IRX5 knockdown restored thermogenesis (a 7-fold increase), and CRISPR-Cas9 repair of rs1421085 restored it in primary adipocytes from a risk-allele carrier (Claussnitzer 2015). This case and the ZRS are experimental results. The viewer's tissue × modality map poses the analogous question, but with predictions, which are hypotheses. For gene expression across individuals, earlier models often fail on the direction of the effect (Sasse 2023; Huang 2023). A non-peer-reviewed preprint finds that the viewer's model agrees only weakly with eQTL effect sizes, with direction concordance only marginally above chance, and that it is better suited to prioritizing fine-mapped variants (Sun 2026).

chapters.title: One letter changes
chapters.kicker: A tiny edit in the text, one big question: does it matter?
chapters.cta: Open the change card and the saturation map

blocks.kid: DNA is the instruction book of your body, like a recipe book with about three billion letters. Some parts are the recipes. In the rest there are, among other things, notes that work like light switches: they say when to read a recipe. Sometimes a letter changes, like "cat" to "cut", or letters go missing. In 2009, almost 9 in 10 signals linked to illnesses and other body features were outside the recipes. Next to the text is a real 3D picture of a tiny machine that reads the book.
blocks.phd: A single-nucleotide variant (SNV) substitutes one base; an indel inserts or deletes bases. In the 2009 genome-wide association study (GWAS) catalog, 88% of trait-associated SNPs (single-nucleotide polymorphisms) were intronic (45%) or intergenic (43%) (Hindorff 2009); in that study they were not overrepresented in introns and were depleted in intergenic regions, so the figure largely reflects that most of the genome is non-coding: protein-coding sequence (CDS) is about {coding_pct}% (range {coding_lo}–{coding_hi}%; our own computation from GENCODE 50 with isoforms merged; the annotation is described in Frankish 2023). Non-coding GWAS signals concentrate in DNase I hypersensitive sites, markers of putative regulatory DNA (Maurano 2012). Association is not causation: the lead SNP is often a tag in linkage disequilibrium with the causal variant, and the signal does not say which cis-regulatory element or gene is involved. Real structure shown: atomic coordinates of PDB 5FLM (experimental structure).

blocks.kid: The viewer gives every change a score called AVI. First, a program from Google DeepMind, AlphaGenome, reads the DNA. It guesses what the change does. Then a second program combines 18 signals, some from the first and some from other data, and gives the score. Imagine a race with every possible change. At 10, the change finishes in the first 10 of every 100. At 20, it finishes first out of 100. At 30, it finishes first out of 1,000. It is an informed guess, not a measurement.
blocks.phd: AVI is the summary score of the viewer's Atlas, developed independently and not endorsed by Google DeepMind. It is not a model output but a neural network trained on AlphaGenome's predictions (Avsec 2026; 1 Mb input) that takes 18 features: 10 regulatory (maxima across tissues of splicing, ATAC, DNase, TF ChIP, histone ChIP, CAGE, PRO-cap, RNA-seq, polyadenylation and contact maps), 4 protein, 2 conservation and 2 indel. That selection is a design decision of the viewer. The training label is a proxy: gnomAD FAF95_GRPMAX, the 95%-confidence filtering allele frequency in the ancestry group where it is highest (among afr, amr, eas, mid, nfe, sas), so common variants stand in for tolerated ones. AVI therefore reflects resemblance to variation that selection does not remove, not a measured functional effect; allele frequency and ancestry are not inputs. SHAP contributions are shown grouped into 4 families. The viewer's own PHRED-style scale, −10·log10(1 − quantile), is logarithmic, with quantiles estimated genome-wide: 10 is the top 10%, 20 the top 1% and 30 the top 0.1%. It ranks for prioritization; it is not an effect size.

blocks.kid: The saturation map tests every possible change in one stretch of the book. The book has only four letters, so each letter can change in three ways. The map tries all three, for 512 letters in a row. Then it paints what the program guesses: where a change matters most, and where it hardly shows. Careful: it guesses for a typical cell, not for you. It helps rank the suspects we already have; the lab checks them. A guess is not a measurement.
blocks.phd: View N1 is a saturation map: 512 positions × 3 alternative bases = 1,536 SNVs, precomputed for two loci (APOA1 and CELSR2). What is painted is the AVI, which takes the maximum across tissues and measures impact, not direction. Card V1 shows APOA1 chr11:116837649 T>G (GRCh38; no rsID in dbSNP 155) at PHRED 25.96: roughly the top 0.25% (about 1 in 400, from the scale's formula). Interpret it with caution: the model predicts, for each reference cell type or tissue, the effect in a typical cell, not in an individual. Earlier models explain expression variation across individuals poorly and often miss the direction of effect (Sasse 2023; Huang 2023). A non-peer-reviewed preprint (Sun 2026, bioRxiv) evaluated Borzoi and AlphaGenome: weak agreement with nominal eQTL effect sizes (Spearman ≤ 0.138), direction only marginally above chance, and better discrimination for fine-mapped variants at PIP ≥ 0.9 (AUROC ≈ 0.82–0.84); it suggests prioritizing already fine-mapped variants rather than using the scores as standalone predictors. AVI was not tested there. A prediction is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

chapters.title: Cut and paste
chapters.kicker: How a cell edits its own instructions, and how a single changed letter could throw off the cut.
chapters.cta: Open the DNM1 splice junctions in the Genome Viewer

blocks.kid: Picture a very long strip of film. Between the good scenes there are bits that never get shown, like ads. Someone cuts out those bits and glues the scenes together, one after another. Your body does this too. Its instructions are a strip written in letters. Each cell cuts away the parts that are not used and glues the parts that are. This cut-and-glue job is called splicing. If a cut goes wrong, the movie ends up with scenes missing, or with extra ones.
blocks.phd: Splicing removes introns from the pre-mRNA and joins the exons; each intron is bounded by a 5′ donor site and a 3′ acceptor site. Unlike most ribonucleoprotein (RNP) enzymes, the spliceosome shows exceptional compositional and structural dynamics through assembly, catalytic activation and active-site remodeling. These dynamics provide accuracy in splice-site recognition and flexibility for alternative splicing, in which one pre-mRNA can give rise to more than one isoform depending on which sites are used (Wahl and Will 2009).

blocks.kid: The scissors in this movie are not scissors. It is a tiny machine. Its pieces snap together just when they are needed. It is called the spliceosome (say SPLY-see-oh-sohm). It looks for the marks that say "ad starts here" and "ad ends here". First it cuts and, at the end, it glues. The picture beside this text is a real structure. Scientists froze the machine and used a special microscope to see its parts. It is a snapshot, just before the last gluing.
blocks.phd: The structure shown beside this chapter (PDB 5XJC; Zhang et al. 2017) is an atomic model of the human spliceosome in the C* state, just before exon ligation, built into a cryo-EM map at an average resolution of 3.76 Å and deposited in the Protein Data Bank. It is a snapshot of a transient state of a complex whose composition changes at every stage (Wahl and Will 2009); it does not represent the ensemble of conformations present in the cell, nor does it explain by itself which sites are chosen. Site choice depends largely on the sequence context around each site, in addition to cellular factors and transcription dynamics. Among its outputs, the model predicts splice-site usage and splice junctions (Avsec et al. 2026; these outputs are described in the paper's main text, not its abstract).

blocks.kid: The machine follows marks on the strip. Sometimes changing one letter is enough to draw a fake mark. The letter may be near the real mark, or far. Now the machine might cut in the wrong place. The Genome Viewer shows an example: the strip called DNM1. There, the changed letter is just seven letters from the mark. It moves one cut by six letters. It changes four joins between scenes. A Google DeepMind artificial-intelligence program calculated this (Avsec et al. 2026). Nobody measured it in a lab.
blocks.phd: As of 2017, deep intronic variants, more than 100 bp from exon-intron junctions, had been described in over 75 disease-associated genes; their most common effect is pseudo-exon inclusion, through activation of non-canonical (cryptic) splice sites or changes in splicing regulatory elements (Vaz-Drago et al. 2017). In the Genome Viewer, the sashimi plot shows the prediction of Google DeepMind's model (Avsec et al. 2026) for chr9:128226027 G>A (GRCh38) in DNM1, in glutamatergic neurons (CL:0000679): it predicts a 6 bp shift of the acceptor site for both upstream donors and changes in four junctions, two gaining usage and two losing it. The variant lies 7 bp from the annotated acceptor: it is not deep intronic, and it illustrates how to read the model output, not the thesis of Vaz-Drago et al. (Own calculation on the Viewer's frozen output; not a published or experimentally validated result.) It is a prediction, not a measurement.

chapters.title: The genome in 3D and the limits of the model
chapters.kicker: When the model predicts no change in the structure, that is a result too.
chapters.cta: See the predicted contact map at CELSR2/PSRC1/SORT1

blocks.kid: Picture DNA, the body's instruction book, as a very long string squeezed into a tiny box. Inside, the string folds into drawers, like the ones in a chest of drawers. Bits in the same drawer touch each other more than bits in different drawers. A tiny helper called CTCF is often found right where a drawer ends. Scientists think it helps close the drawer. A contact map uses colors to show which bits of the string touch. The strongest touches look like mountains.
blocks.phd: Hi-C maps show that the genome folds into domains: regions where interactions are more frequent within than between domains. Dixon et al. 2012 described megabase-scale "topological domains" (TADs), stable across cell types and conserved across species, with boundaries enriched for CTCF. Rao et al. 2014, using in situ Hi-C at 1 kb resolution (4.9 billion contacts in GM12878), defined contact domains with a median length of 185 kb (not one-to-one equivalent to the TADs of Dixon et al.) and about 10,000 loops linking promoters and enhancers; at loop anchors, CTCF sites occur in a convergent orientation in more than 90% of cases. Dixon et al. suggested that CTCF "may have a role" at the boundaries; that CTCF establishes them is a hypothesis consistent with these data, and enrichment alone does not demonstrate it.

blocks.kid: A big change in the DNA can break the edge of a drawer and mix up two drawers. Then the hands and feet of some children form differently. Here we look at a change of just one letter, near CELSR2, PSRC1 and SORT1. The map the model predicts hardly moves: the biggest change is 1.46% of the gap between the highest and lowest points of the map from before. Maybe the problem is not in the folding, though the model can be wrong.
blocks.phd: Lupiáñez et al. 2015 showed that deletions, inversions and duplications at the WNT6/IHH/EPHA4/PAX3 locus rewire long-range enhancer–promoter interactions and cause limb malformations, but only when the variant disrupts a CTCF-associated boundary. In the Genome Viewer, the underlying model's predictions (Avsec et al. 2026, Google DeepMind) for rs12740374 (GRCh38 chr1:109274968 G>T, CELSR2–PSRC1–SORT1 locus) in HepG2 show no appreciable remodeling: the maximum |ALT−REF| change across the 1 Mb window is 1.46% of the reference map's dynamic range (max−min), on a log scale (in-house calculation). All 28 available contact tracks come from cell lines, none from primary tissue, and a predicted absence of change does not prove an absence of real change. This is consistent with a mechanism that does not act through 3D architecture, but this chapter does not demonstrate it.

blocks.kid:
A variant is a difference in DNA; many are one-letter changes. The model is like a weather forecast: it tells you where to look first, not what will happen at your house.

It can help choose variants to check first. It is weak at saying how much something changes in one person, and often wrong about whether it goes up or down. We know little about how it works for people all over the world. Treat each prediction as a good question, not as an answer.
blocks.phd:
Huang et al. 2023 (four deep-learning models) found limited performance in explaining expression variation across individuals, with frequent failures in the direction of effect. Sasse et al. 2023 (839 individuals, ROSMAP) point out that the methods then available did not predict the direction of variant effects well. Both studies predate AlphaGenome and did not evaluate it. Sun et al. 2026, a preprint without peer review, evaluated Borzoi and AlphaGenome (the model behind the predictions in the Genome Viewer) and found weak agreement with nominal eQTL effect sizes (Spearman ≤ 0.138) and direction concordance only marginally above chance. Discrimination is better for fine-mapped variants at PIP ≥ 0.9 (distance-matched AUROC, African American set: 0.837 [0.790–0.870] Borzoi; 0.820 [0.793–0.845] AlphaGenome), which the authors attribute to fine-mapping resolution, LD and annotation composition. They recommend using these scores as prioritization evidence for fine-mapped variants, not as standalone predictors of eQTL effect size.

This model predicts what a reference cell type does, on average. It is strong at ranking which variants deserve investigation and weak at telling you the size —and sometimes the direction— of the effect in a specific person. The training data are skewed toward European ancestry. Treat a prediction as a hypothesis, not as a measurement.
